notes.notes: The page provides general framework context useful to a skill-page extraction agent. It explains the structure of the SFIA framework, including the seven levels of responsibility and the generic attributes that describe behavioural factors. The page also discusses the updates made in SFIA 9, including the addition of new skills and the refinement of existing ones. Additionally, it provides information on how to navigate the SFIA framework and how to adopt SFIA 9. The page also mentions the SFIA ecosystem, which includes user guidance, mappings to industry frameworks, and links to industry bodies of knowledge. Overall, the page provides a comprehensive overview of the SFIA framework and its updates, which would be useful for an agent extracting per-level skill descriptions from the skill pages.

The page provides an overview of the SFIA 9 full framework view, which includes every skill in SFIA 9 organized into categories and subcategories. It also mentions the use of this view for the SFIA complete reference guide, the A3 summary sheet, and basic navigation. Additionally, the page links to other relevant pages, such as the SFIA 9 skills directory A-Z, levels of responsibility, and SFIA skills profiles. The page also provides information about the SFIA Foundation, a global not-for-profit organization that oversees the production and use of the Skills Framework for the Information Age. The links to other pages, such as 'How SFIA works - Levels of responsibility and skills' and 'Why SFIA skills are not defined at all 7 levels', suggest that the page is part of a larger framework that provides context and guidance for using SFIA. The page's content is relevant to understanding the structure and organization of the SFIA framework, which could be useful for an agent extracting per-level skill descriptions from skill pages.

The page provides information about the SFIA 9 framework, including its structure, levels of responsibility, and skills. It also explains how SFIA works, why skills are not defined at all 7 levels, and the context for SFIA. Additionally, it offers downloadable documents, such as reference PDFs and an Excel spreadsheet, which contain the complete text of SFIA 9 skill descriptions, levels of responsibilities, generic attributes, and behavioural factors. The page also outlines the licensing system for using SFIA, including the free licence for personal career development and internal use by employers, as well as the modest licence fee for large organisations and commercial purposes. The SFIA Foundation is a not-for-profit organisation that maintains and distributes SFIA, and the licence fee supports the continued development of the framework and ecosystem support.

This information is useful for understanding the framework context and how skills are defined and structured within SFIA.

The SFIA framework defines 7 levels of responsibility, each with distinct attributes. These levels are: 
1 - Follows, 2 - Assists, 3 - Applies, 4 - Enables, 5 - Ensures, 6 - Initiates, and 7 - Sets strategy. 
Understanding these levels and their attributes is crucial for extracting per-level skill descriptions.

Not all skills are defined at every level. This is because some skills may not be relevant or may not require differentiation at certain levels. The framework provides explanations for why skills are not defined at all 7 levels.

Each skill page is structured to provide information on the skill, including a description, and level-specific descriptions where applicable. The level-specific descriptions outline the expectations and responsibilities associated with each level.

Key framework terminology includes "skills", "levels of responsibility", and "attributes". Skills refer to the specific abilities or competencies, while levels of responsibility define the degree of expertise, accountability, and decision-making authority. Attributes describe the characteristics and expectations associated with each level.

When extracting per-level skill descriptions, agents should navigate to the relevant skill page and look for level-specific descriptions. The "Levels of responsibility" section and explanations for why skills are not defined at all levels can provide valuable context for understanding the framework and accurately extracting skill descriptions.
